Multiple procedures may exist for heating with the receiver assembly depending on the specific operation and internal tank temperature measurements. Based on observed operational data, the largest thermal gradients occur during the air preheating and initial salt fill steps; in addition, the tank is susceptible to buckling during these steps due to the low (or zero) inventory level. For these reasons, the first two steps of the commissioning process are considered the most critical for analysis. 3.2.1 Air Preheating Process The air preheating step is performed with a temporary propane- or natural gas-fired hot-air blower. Air is introduced into the tank through a nozzle(s) on the roof and exits the tank through a nozzle that extends from the roof into the tank. It is desirable to use specialized nozzles for the air inlet and outlets to control the preheating airflow. The air inlet temperature is controlled based on skin-point temperature measurements within the tank and the air inlet temperature. Depending on the tank geometry, different control strategies may be appropriate. Based on the parametric studies performed under this award [4,19], temperature differences of 40°C or more can cause permanent damage to the floor; therefore, the floor's temperature is estimated to be a maximum of 35°C. The goal is to perform the initial fill at a relatively constant temperature while minimizing thermal gradients in the tank; however, there is no mechanism to control thermal gradients once salt begins flowing into the tank. Heat losses and the salt inlet temperature will drive the temperature gradient in the tank. To help with this process, the salt inlet temperature can be stabilized with an in-line heater, if available; otherwise, the inlet temperature will be determined by the cold tank temperature and the heat losses through the piping.
